# Vendelux raises its Series B to power the future of B2B events

Michael Goerlitz

Published On :

July 8, 2026

Updated On :

July 22, 2026

 

As AI transforms how companies create content and engage buyers, human connection is becoming an even more important part of the customer journey. To build authentic relationships, companies are pouring billions back into events where human-to-human conversations can move business deals forward. However, most event programs still run on gut instinct, so teams back the wrong events and walk away without measurable results or the ability to defend their spend.

Vendelux was built to change that. Today we’re announcing our $50M Series B, led by Tribeca Venture Partners, with participation from S3, Pelion Ventures, HubSpot Ventures, FirstMark, and Cervin Ventures. This brings our total funding to $71M.

Vendelux provides the infrastructure to take the guesswork out of in-person engagement by tracking more than 250,000 global B2B events. Vendelux helps companies identify where their buyers will be, who they should meet, and how to create meaningful business relationships. Whether you’re an AI native startup or a global enterprise, the goal is the same: human connection at scale. Vendelux is the intelligence layer that connects every participant in the B2B event ecosystem – from marketers and sales teams to event organizers – making events more measurable, more connected, and more valuable for everyone involved.

More than 50,000 marketing professionals use Vendelux, and the platform has influenced over $5 billion in event spend. As event budgets continue to grow, marketers are demanding the same level of intelligence, measurement, and accountability from events that they expect from every other marketing channel. Companies like Ramp, Glean, Coupa, McKesson, WRITER, Deel, Intel, and the United States Postal Service use the platform to turn their event programs into a measurable revenue channel.

We love their ambition to define how modern companies run their event programs.”

Our mission is to help companies create those connections more effectively by bringing data, intelligence, and measurement to an industry that has historically relied on instinct. Since our Series A, we’ve built the leading intelligence platform for B2B events. With this new round of funding, we’re investing in AI and building products that bring marketers and event organizers closer together, helping every participant get more value from every event.”

# Event Marketing in 2026: A Buyer-Voice Playbook for Making Events Accountable

We’ve spent the last 30 months listening to how B2B buyers actually talk about event marketing. Across over 2,500 prospect and customer conversations, one pattern keeps rising to the top: the next decade of event marketing is decided by attribution, not attendance. Buyers don’t ask whether events work anymore. They ask which ones drove pipeline, and most can’t answer with confidence. This guide is what we’ve learned from those conversations, layered onto seven years of historical attendance data covering 250,000+ B2B events. It’s written for the marketers, RevOps leaders, and sales execs who need event marketing to be a forecastable channel, not a line item their CFO questions every January.

## Table of contents

- What is event marketing?
- Why measurement is the new event marketing battle
- How to actually measure event marketing ROI
- The five core event marketing KPIs
- Event marketing strategy: a 12-phase framework
- B2B event marketing: where this looks different from B2C
- Event marketing platforms vs event management platforms
- The role of attribution in event marketing
- Frequently asked questions

## What is event marketing?

Event marketing is how B2B companies use conferences, trade shows, roadshows, hosted dinners, and sponsored activations to move prospects toward a buying decision. Done well, it produces measurable pipeline. Done poorly, it produces lanyards and stories.

In the narrowest sense, event marketing means promoting your own event. In the broader and more useful sense (the one this guide uses throughout), it covers every paid or earned presence at an event where your buyers actually show up, including:

- Conferences and trade shows where your prospects assemble for industry programming.
- Sponsorships and activations ranging from booths to keynote slots to sponsored cocktail hours.
- Field marketing programs: regional dinners, executive briefings, roadshows that bring the conversation to specific accounts in specific cities.
- Owned events and hosted programs: your dinner, your roundtable, your private breakfast on the sidelines of a major industry conference, or a stand-alone event in a city where you know your top accounts will be that week.

The job is the same across formats: get the right people in the room and turn the conversation into a meeting that books pipeline. Everything else (the booth, the swag, the panel topic) is plumbing.

## Why measurement is the new event marketing battle

For most of the last two decades, B2B event marketing was the most-spent, least-measured line item in the marketing budget. Companies wrote checks because their competitors did, and because their best customers seemed to come from somewhere in the trade show calendar. Pipeline attribution was guesswork, and everyone basically knew it.

That tolerance is gone. In 2026, the dominant theme across the conversations we have with buyers is no longer “can events drive growth?”. It’s “prove this is worth doubling down on, or I’m cutting it.”

“This is pretty much a tool that every company in the future is going to need. Because at the moment you utilize CRM and every other type of tools to help you forecast and make data-driven decisions. And the event space, there’s nothing like that to do that.”

Source: a head of demand gen at a mid-market technology company

When we ask buyers how they’re measuring events today, the same words keep coming up: “guesswork,” “internal analytics you can spin however you want,” “a deck the team puts together after the show that nobody really trusts.” A second pattern shows up right next to the measurement problem: budget defensibility.

“My biggest goal is to have proof on a paper to say this makes sense from two of our go to markets or even all three of our go to markets that we need to be there from a big perspective.”

Source: a marketing leader at an enterprise B2B SaaS company

Looking back across the conversations, the buyer’s question has shifted. In 2023 and early 2024, buyers asked us “what does this do?”. By 2026-Q1, it’s “how does this compare to our existing stack, and how does it prove ROI in a way our CFO accepts?” Buyers have moved past curiosity and gotten serious about accountability, and the programs that can meet them there are the ones still in business in 2027.

This is the throughline of every section that follows. The strategy choices, the KPIs, the platform decisions, the attribution models, they’ve all got to answer one question now: does this make events a forecastable channel?

## How to actually measure event marketing ROI

There are roughly a hundred frameworks online for “event marketing ROI.” Most of them stop at (pipeline generated ÷ event cost) and call it done. The math is fine; it’s the inputs where every program falls apart. You can’t measure event ROI honestly without three things working together:

1. Predicted-attendee intelligence weeks before the event happens. Confirmed registration lists from the organizer usually arrive too close to the event (if they’re shared at all), and the conference networking app only opens during the event itself. By the time you find a name worth meeting, the prospect’s calendar’s already gone. What your team actually needs is predicted-attendee data, forecasts of who’s likely to attend based on seven years of historical attendance patterns, public registration signals, and stated commitments, eight to twelve weeks ahead, while there’s still time to book.
2. Meetings booked into your sales team’s calendar before anyone walks into the venue. A booth scan and a coffee in passing aren’t pipeline-creating events. A scheduled, qualified meeting on a calendar with a decision-maker, in a private setting, before or during the conference, is. The hardest part isn’t the meeting itself; it’s the outbound work to find the right person, sequence them properly, and lock in the calendar invite weeks ahead. Programs that win the measurement battle either staff their SDR team to do this at scale or run it through a managed Meetings service whose only job is to book the meetings on the program’s behalf. Either way, the goal’s the same: your reps show up at the event with a full calendar of ICP-fit meetings instead of a list of names to chase.
3. CRM-attributed pipeline downstream. Every meeting needs to flow back into HubSpot or Salesforce with the event tagged as the source. Without that loop closed, the finance team can’t see event-sourced revenue and the program defaults back to “brand spend” in next year’s budget review.

“I would love to have the concrete other than our own internal analytics, which I think can be spun however many different ways you want to look at it.”

Source: a head of field marketing at an enterprise B2B SaaS company

The vendors and operators winning the measurement battle in 2026 are the ones giving buyers all three at the same time: pre-event attendee intelligence, an outbound meeting-booking layer that fills the calendar, and CRM integration that closes the loop. Our platform at Vendelux is built around exactly this stack, but the pattern matters more than the vendor. If you’re running events without all three pieces in place, the ROI math doesn’t compute.

## The five core event marketing KPIs

Pipeline is the headline number, but it’s not the only KPI worth tracking. The five we recommend treating as the operating dashboard for any B2B event program:

1. ICP-fit meetings booked, count of scheduled, qualified meetings with ICP-matching titles at ICP-matching accounts. The leading indicator of pipeline.
2. Event-sourced pipeline ($), net-new opportunity dollars where the event is the first-touch or attributed source in CRM.
3. Event-influenced pipeline ($), opportunity dollars where the event appears anywhere in the multi-touch attribution path. Always larger than event-sourced; useful for telling the full story to finance.
4. Cost per ICP meeting, total event spend (badge, travel, sponsorship, T&E) divided by ICP-fit meetings booked. The unit economic that lets you compare events to each other and to other channels.
5. Closed-won revenue attributed to the event, the lagging indicator. Track it 60, 180, and 365 days post-event so the program isn’t judged on a 30-day window that always looks worse than reality.

Secondary KPIs worth instrumenting once the core five are in place: booth scans, demos delivered, content downloads, sales-accepted opportunities, and meetings booked per SDR hour invested. Secondary metrics tell the how story; the core five tell the whether story.

## Event marketing strategy: a 12-phase framework

A working event marketing strategy is less of a 50-slide deck and more of a repeatable operating rhythm. The 12 phases we see in every program that actually scales:

Annual planning (Q4 of the prior year): 1. Define the year’s ICP and revenue targets. 2. Build the candidate event list using historical attendance data, not gut feel. Score candidate events by how many of your ICP accounts have historically attended. 3. Score and rank events by projected ICP density and projected pipeline. 4. Allocate budget by event tier.

Pre-event (8–12 weeks out): 5. Pull predicted-attendee data for each event and shortlist target accounts. 6. Begin outbound, calibrated to where the prospect sits in the funnel. 7. Confirm meetings to a calendar with venue, time, and agenda. By T-minus-2-weeks, your reps’ calendars should already be 70%+ booked.

At the event (week-of): 8. Run the meeting machine: sales reps in suites and hosted-meeting rooms, not on the show floor chasing scans. 9. Capture every interaction in CRM in real time. 10. Host one anchor activation (dinner, roundtable, private breakfast) for top-tier accounts. Use predicted-attendee data to know exactly who’ll be in town that week so the invitations land.

# Event Marketing Tools: The B2B Operator’s Stack Guide

Author :

Stefan Deeran

Published On :

May 27, 2026

The event marketing tool stack is bigger than most operators realize and smaller than most vendors imply. There’s no single “event marketing platform” that handles attendee research, outreach, on-site execution, and attribution. There are categories of tools, each solving a specific job. The teams that run lean and high-performing event programs pick one tool per category and integrate them deliberately.

This guide is a category-by-category walkthrough of the event marketing tool stack. It doesn’t rank specific products head-to-head; it explains what each category does, what to evaluate, and how the categories should connect. It pulls from over 2,500 B2B buyer conversations our team has analyzed across the last 30 months.

### Get attendee data for any B2B event

Attendee lists for 250,000+ events, filtered to your ICP.

Get the Data

## Table of contents

1. The event marketing tool stack at a glance
2. Category 1: event intelligence and attendee research
3. Category 2: event management and registration platforms
4. Category 3: outreach and meeting booking
5. Category 4: lead capture and on-site execution
6. Category 5: CRM and attribution

8. Category 7: AI assistants for campaign creation
9. How the stack should integrate
10. Common stack mistakes

## The event marketing tool stack at a glance

A complete B2B event marketing stack has seven layers:

1. Event intelligence: which events matter, who’s attending
2. Event management: registration, agenda, owned-event ops
3. Outreach + meeting booking: pre-event cadences, calendar coordination
4. Lead capture: on-site scan, qualification, conversation notes
5. CRM + attribution: Campaign records, opportunity tagging
6. Analytics + reporting: dashboards, ROI math
7. AI assistants: campaign creation, content drafting

Some platforms span multiple layers. Most don’t. The mistake we see most often: teams buy a “platform” that promises to do all seven layers, end up using it well at one, and force-fit the rest. The better approach is to pick the best tool for each layer and integrate them.

## Category 1: event intelligence and attendee research

### What this category does

Tells you which events your ICP attends, which target accounts will be there, and how confident the attendance prediction is. The category includes both flagship industry conferences and the long tail of regional, niche, and ancillary events.

### What to evaluate

- Coverage: how many events tracked, how often updated
- Account-level intelligence: can you filter by your target account list
- Confidence tiers: does the platform distinguish Confirmed from Predicted from Historic
- Late-cycle data: does the platform capture the final 10 days of registration growth
- Integration: push to CRM as Campaign Members or Segments
- Outreach automation: built-in campaign creation or external

### Why this category is foundational

Without attendee intelligence, the rest of the stack is guessing. You can’t run a pre-event Meetings cadence if you don’t know who’s attending. You can’t pick the right events if you don’t know which ones have your target accounts. Vendelux operates in this category. For a deeper comparison of platforms in this layer, see our best event marketing platforms guide.

## Category 2: event management and registration platforms

### What this category does

Runs your owned events: registration pages, ticketing, agenda, session management, attendee communications, post-event surveys. Some platforms also support virtual and hybrid event production.

### What to evaluate

- Registration UX: how good is the attendee experience
- Customization: can you brand the registration flow
- Session and agenda management: speakers, tracks, sponsors
- Hybrid and virtual support: if relevant
- CRM integration: registration data flows automatically to Salesforce/HubSpot
- Reporting: registration analytics, attendance reporting

### When you need it

If you run owned events (user conferences, executive summits, roadshows), you need a platform in this category. If you only sponsor third-party events, you can often skip this category and use simpler form/CRM tooling for any needed registration.

## Category 3: outreach and meeting booking

### What this category does

Runs the pre-event email cadence, schedules calls, coordinates meeting calendars, and handles the cold call cadence for booking pre-event meetings.

### What to evaluate

- Cadence sophistication: multi-touch, multi-channel (email + call + LinkedIn)
- Calendar coordination: can it book meetings against multiple AE calendars without conflicts
- CRM logging: every touch logged against the contact record
- Cold call support: integrated dialer or just email
- Reply parsing: can it route positive replies vs. negative replies automatically

### Who runs it

In-house BDR/SDR teams using a sequencing platform (Outreach, Salesloft, Apollo for outbound, etc.) or a managed Meetings team (Vendelux runs one) that brings the cadence and the execution together. For the cadence playbook itself, see our event email marketing guide.

The decision factor is opportunity cost. If your BDR team has the time to hold the 28-day cadence consistently across 10-20 events per year, run it in-house. If they’re constantly being pulled into the next quarter’s pipeline target, outsource to a Meetings team.

## Category 4: lead capture and on-site execution

### What this category does

Captures booth scans, walk-up conversations, and qualified leads on-site. Tags each capture with qualification level, conversation notes, and next-action data. Pushes the captured leads to CRM in real time.

### What to evaluate

- Mobile-friendly scan interface: booth staff need this on phones or tablets
- Custom fields: qualification tag, conversation notes, next-action date
- Real-time CRM push: same-day, not batch upload after the show
- Offline support: booth Wi-Fi is unreliable
- Multi-event support: you’ll use this across many shows per year

### Why most teams underinvest here

Event organizers usually offer a scanner with the badge package. Most teams use it and skip the dedicated lead capture app. The organizer scanner captures name and email. It doesn’t capture qualification tag or conversation notes. Post-show triage takes a week instead of a day. A purpose-built lead capture app is worth the setup cost.

## Category 5: CRM and attribution

### What this category does

This is your Salesforce or HubSpot instance. Event marketing tools push data into the CRM; the CRM holds the attribution model and reports.

### What to evaluate

The CRM itself is rarely an event marketing decision (you already have one). What matters is how it’s configured:

- Campaign per event: every event gets a Salesforce Campaign or HubSpot list
- Campaign Member status workflow: Registered, Attended, Met, Hot, etc.
- Opportunity source tagging: opportunities created from event-touched contacts carry the event tag
- Multi-touch attribution model: event credit doesn’t get washed out by later touches
- Closed-won loop: closed-won deals trace back to Campaign source

### Integration with attendee intelligence

Vendelux pushes Segments to CRM as Campaign Members (Salesforce) or list members (HubSpot). New Confirmed and Late Confirmed attendees flow in automatically. Lead capture from the booth adds to the same Campaign. The attribution chain stays intact end-to-end. For the full attribution-model breakdown, see our event marketing attribution guide. For ROI math, see our event marketing ROI guide.

### Get attendee data for any B2B event

Attendee lists for 250,000+ events, filtered to your ICP.

Get the Data

## Category 6: analytics and reporting

### What this category does

Aggregates data across CRM, the event intelligence platform, the lead capture app, and the outreach platform. Produces dashboards showing pipeline-per-event, cost-per-meeting, closed-won attribution, and ROI math.

### What to evaluate

- Cross-tool data joins: event Campaign data + opportunity data + cost data
- Pipeline reporting cadence: 60/180/365-day automation
- Cost-per-meeting math: automated calculation from CRM + event spend
- Custom dashboards: the finance partner’s view vs. the marketing operator’s view

### Who builds this

In most B2B orgs, analytics and reporting is a RevOps function rather than a marketing function. Marketing provides the inputs (events, costs, Campaigns); RevOps builds the dashboards. The split works when both teams agree on the attribution model upfront.

## Category 7: AI assistants for campaign creation

### What this category does

Generates pre-event email cadences, outreach copy, follow-up sequences, and content drafts from a single brief. Reduces the time-to-launch for a new event from days to minutes.

### What to evaluate

- Output quality: does the copy sound like a human wrote it, or like a template
- Customization to your voice: can it match your brand and tone
- Knowledge of your product: can it reference your value props correctly
- Integration with the cadence platform: does the output ship straight to Outreach/Salesloft, or do you copy-paste

### Vendelux’s ChatVDX

ChatVDX is built into the Vendelux platform. You describe the event, the offer, and the ICP. It generates three sub-campaigns (Early Confirmed, All Predicted, Late Confirmed). Output is ready for review and execution. The time savings is what lets teams run disciplined cadences across many events per year without burning out the team that writes the copy.

- Event intelligence → CRM (Segments push as Campaign Members or list members)
- Outreach → CRM (every touch logs against the contact record)

## How Vendelux Keeps Your Event Data Safe

Event Tech Summary Vendelux, the intelligence layer for the B2B event ecosystem, meets the highest data protection standards, SOC 2, GDPR, the Data Privacy Framework, and CCPA, so brands can turn in-person experiences into measurable revenue compliantly and confidently. Key Takeaways We meet global best practices to keep your data safe: Vendelux operates under SOC 2, GDPR, the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework (DPF), and CCPA/CPRA. We also explain what these protections actually require and cover. We have common-sense safeguards that'll keep your infosec team happy: Platform safeguards include multi-factor authentication (MFA), single sign-on (SSO) for enterprise identity providers, and attendee name obfuscation as a default privacy control. Safety and information is balanced so you can still use data to inform your event strategy: Attendee name obfuscation limits exposure of individual attendee PII (Personally Identifiable Information) while preserving the company-, role-, and seniority-level intelligence marketers and sales teams actually act on. Event organizers, we've got your back, too: Organizers can feel confident about how we meet compliance obligations (consent, data processing agreements, retention). See our companion guide for more: GDPR & CCPA Compliance in Event Data Capture. For years, the digital business world has had intelligence and the physical one hasn't. Companies know who visits their site, who clicks an ad, which accounts are showing intent. But the rooms where B2B relationships actually get built, the summits, conferences, and dinners, have stayed largely opaque. Vendelux exists to close that gap. Our platform helps marketers prove and grow measurable revenue from events. As an event intelligence platform tracking more than 250,000 global B2B events, we help companies understand where their buyers will be, who they should meet, and how to turn those moments into measurable revenue. Vendelux spent the last several years building that data infrastructure: about events, about companies, and about the people who attend them. In order to do that, our platform must both connect the disparate data missing from the industry and also have safeguards on how this data is stored and used. Data Compliance for a Global Event Ecosystem Data protection is infrastructure that has to be built well in order to be useful to anyone. We operate from the following frameworks to better serve marketing leaders, no matter where they are, at the highest possible global standard. For event organizers: this reflects the same standard you'd expect from any vendor entrusted with your attendees' data. It's what allows you to continue sharing event intelligence with confidence, without putting your audience's trust in you at risk. For brands and marketers: this is what should allow your security and legal teams to approve Vendelux without friction. Most event marketing examples roundups are show-and-tell: pretty booths, branded swag, viral activations. This one’s different. The 12 examples below are B2B programs that produced measurable pipeline, sourced from a mix of Vendelux’s published customer case studies and the patterns we’ve seen across 2,500+ B2B buyer conversations in the last 30 months. ## Conference sponsorships that produced pipeline

### Example 1: Voltage tripled its late-stage pipeline

Format: Tier-1 conference sponsorship with full operational rigor (predicted-attendee intelligence, pre-event meeting booking, anchor activation, CRM attribution).

Outcome: Voltage documented a 300% increase in late-stage pipeline after operationalizing the meeting-booking layer alongside their sponsorship investments. The pipeline number wasn’t a one-off; it sustained across multiple events as the operational pattern repeated.

Replicable pattern: the multiplier on a Tier-1 sponsorship isn’t the sponsorship fee, it’s whether the pre-event meeting calendar gets filled before the event opens. Voltage’s program structured the meeting-booking layer as a non-optional input, not a nice-to-have, which is what flipped the ROI math.

### Example 2: Rocketium booked 12 meetings at a single conference

Format: Tier-1 European industry conference (DMEXCO) with predicted-attendee data driving pre-event outreach to target accounts.

Outcome: Rocketium doubled pre-event meetings compared to previous editions and booked 12 confirmed meetings at the conference, with several converting to opportunities in the 60 days after the event.

Replicable pattern: the per-meeting math works for international conferences too. Rocketium proved that the predicted-attendee playbook isn’t US-specific; it transfers to any major industry conference where the buyer-density math holds up.

### Example 3: A mid-market cybersecurity company at a major industry conference

Format: Tier-1 cybersecurity conference sponsorship with a private dinner the night before the main event, attendees pulled from the predicted-attendee list of CISOs at $1B+ companies.

Outcome: 22 confirmed dinner attendees out of 28 invited. 8 of the 22 were target accounts that had been stuck in outbound sequence for months prior to the conference. 3 of those 8 became opportunities within 60 days post-event.

Replicable pattern: Tier-1 sponsorships outperform when the anchor activation is curated to a specific buyer persona (CISOs, in this case) and the invite list is built from accounts already in your outbound funnel. The dinner becomes the meeting-acceleration mechanism for stalled deals.

## Owned events and side dinners

### Example 4: Superhuman’s SXSW activation

Format: Superhuman ran an event-selection-driven program at SXSW focused on filling high-value seats with the right attendee mix rather than maximizing total attendance.

Outcome: The selection rigor produced a meaningfully higher-quality conversation set at the event, which translated to a measurable lift in the post-event pipeline. The case study covers the specific framework Superhuman used to score events and predict which attendees would actually show up.

Replicable pattern: quality of seat-fill beats quantity of seat-fill in B2B owned events. Programs that select event attendees with the same rigor they apply to sales-call prospecting consistently outperform programs that try to fill the room by volume.

### Example 5: A B2B SaaS company hosting a 22-person side dinner

Format: Private dinner the night before a major industry conference, with attendees pulled from the predicted-attendee list of that conference. The dinner was hosted at a named restaurant, the host list included two existing customers acting as references, and the invite came from the host company’s CEO.

Outcome: 22 confirmed attendees out of 28 invited (79 percent fill rate). 5 of the attendees accepted because of the social proof of who else was on the guest list. Of those 5, 3 became opportunities within 60 days. Total dinner cost: roughly $18,000 all-in. Pipeline produced: well above the cost-per-meeting benchmark for the company’s other channels.

Replicable pattern: side dinners alongside major conferences are the highest-per-dollar event format for most B2B programs. The leverage is the conference’s natural ICP density without paying the conference’s sponsorship premium.

### Example 6: A devtools company’s executive-briefing program

Format: 1-on-1 executive briefings in the buyer’s city, with the buyer’s full evaluation committee present, the host company’s CTO leading the discussion, and two reference customers joining via video for the technical-validation portion.

Outcome: Average deal advanced from “evaluation” to “verbal” within 30 days of the briefing when the program was executed correctly. Used as the last-mile mechanic for any enterprise deal stuck at the technical-validation stage.

Replicable pattern: executive briefings work as deal accelerants, not as net-new pipeline generators. The math is different from sponsorships or dinners: lower volume, higher deal velocity per touch. By Alex Reynolds, Co-Founder and CEO, Vendelux

Six years ago I joined Shutterstock’s business development team to work on all kinds of opportunities, from marketing partnerships with West Elm showcasing our premium content in stores, to new market strategy in China, and general build/buy/partner analysis. The team was also responsible for our 3rd party integrations strategy, including our native API partnerships into platforms such as Facebook Ads and Wix.

It became apparent very quickly that this API business was a massive opportunity for Shutterstock and we needed to invest in this area. In 2017, the executive team accepted our proposal to create a dedicated business unit for API partnerships called Platform Solutions. Since then, we built a 75 person, eight figure ARR business as intropreneurs within a public company.

Building and scaling this team was the most challenging and exciting experience of my career. I’ve grown tremendously as a leader and have worked with the most incredible team. I wouldn’t trade it for the world!

While building this business, we saw that going to in-person events and conferences was one of the best ways to generate new business and move existing partnerships along. Or at least, it could be, if we sent the right people to the right events. However, if we went to the wrong events, or even if we sent the wrong people to a good event, it was a big waste of time, energy, and money. There was also a huge opportunity cost for missing out on great events, where we would find out about something the week of and kick ourselves for not knowing sooner.

We realized that it was critical to know about all of the relevant events, and understand who was going to be attending, in order to optimize which events to attend and who to send. The problem? There was no platform to help us with this challenge! We built complex processes, hired external data companies, and spent hours googling, and we were still not at the scale or precision that we wanted. We knew there had to be a better way.

It turns out that we were not alone. Many companies struggle with the same problem and related problems. For example, 70% of B2B professionals find it difficult to drive pipeline from events, and less than 20% of event marketers can calculate ROI from events.

Companies are spending 30% of their marketing budgets on the event marketing channel, and the best companies drive 40%+ pipeline from events, but there is no platform to help maximize revenue from this channel. No single platform to help with the end to end journey, from determining the right events and scheduling meetings, to automatically tracking impact from the channel. So after leaving Shutterstock last year and taking some time to reflect on this space, we decided to build it!

Introducing Vendelux, a platform that empowers event marketers to maximize impact from the event marketing channel. We have built a database of over 30,000 events and are leveraging CRM pipeline data to help companies determine the best events to attend and sponsor, and who to send, to maximize revenue from the channel. This Event Intelligence offering is the first step towards building the System of Record for the Event Marketing Channel.

I loved building a start-up as an intropreneur within Shutterstock. Loved moving quickly, failing fast, scaling the team, getting in the trenches, and living on the cutting edge of innovation for the company. I could not be more excited to officially dive into the deep end and build an independent start-up as an entrepreneur. The early response has been incredible and we are just getting started!

Vendelux is transforming how companies discover, evaluate, and maximize the impact of events.

Event marketers are the driving force behind pipeline and brand — yet events remain one of the least optimized and most opaque marketing channels. Vendelux changes that. We provide the system of record for event marketing, giving teams the data and insights they need to make smarter, more strategic decisions.

Our AI-powered platform delivers proprietary insights across 250,000+ events, helping high-growth companies identify where their ideal customers will be, maximize ROI, and turn events into a scalable growth channel. Customers often describe Vendelux as an event marketer’s dream. A key part of this is our growing network of event organizer partnerships — where organizers share first-party attendee and sponsorship data, and in return gain access to valuable market insights.

In addition, Vendelux Meetings helps customers turn event insights into action — using AI to identify high-value attendees and automatically book 1:1 meetings with the right prospects at conferences. This allows teams to maximize pipeline generation and make every event materially more impactful.

Founded in 2021, Vendelux is a Series A SaaS company backed by leading investors including FirstMark, with a recent $14M round. Our team brings experience from companies like Bain, ZoomInfo, Airbnb, FanDuel, Shutterstock, Compass and more.

We're hiring a Head of Meetings Operations to own and scale the engine behind one of Vendelux's fastest-growing products: a fully managed meetings service that generates thousands of qualified meetings per month for our customers.

You'll own the people, the process, the operational infrastructure, and the product requirements that power customer outcomes. You'll lead a team of Campaign Managers and cold callers, build the systems that make outreach predictable and scalable, and serve as the connective tissue between execution, customer success, and product development.

You're comfortable operating at both 5,000 feet and 5 feet. You can design a strategic operating model in the morning and diagnose why a campaign's show rate dropped in the afternoon. You don't wait to be told what's broken—you build the systems that surface problems before they escalate.

### Lead & Develop the Meetings Team

- Manage, coach, and develop a team of Campaign Managers and cold callers.
- Build a culture of ownership and accountability—shifting from reactive task execution to proactive, quality-driven performance.
- Set clear performance standards across volume and quality metrics; create visibility and accountability without relying on pressure tactics.

### Own the End-to-End Outreach Engine

- Define strategy and best practices for targeting, sequencing, personalization, and multi-channel engagement across email, cold calling, LinkedIn, and emerging channels.
- Own the full campaign lifecycle—from launch to QA to performance review—ensuring campaigns hit quality standards and scale efficiently across 200+ customers.
- Own meeting quality end-to-end — ensuring every campaign delivers genuine value to customers, and build the feedback loops and playbooks that make high-quality outcomes repeatable at scale.

### Drive Operational Excellence

- Build the systems, SOPs, and SLA tracking that make execution predictable at scale—removing manual bottlenecks faster than the business creates them.
- Use AI tools and automation to reduce oversight burden and free Campaign Managers from tactical work so they can focus on strategic optimization.
- Define the KPIs, dashboards, and alerting that surface problems before they escalate—giving leadership and customers real-time confidence in campaign health.

### Own Product & Cross-Functional Requirements

- Serve as the primary voice of the Meetings product internally—translating operational pain points and customer outcomes into clear product and automation requirements for Engineering and Product.
- Partner with Customer Success to align on customer goals, onboarding, and campaign performance.
- Bring insights back to the business to improve product, messaging, and GTM strategy.

### What We're Looking For

- 8+ years in Operations, or roles involving process design, cross-functional coordination, and team management.
- Proven success building and scaling operating models in a fast-paced, high-growth environment—ideally from early-stage foundations.
- Strong people manager with experience developing frontline execution teams
- Familiarity with B2B cold outreach mechanics—email deliverability, cold calling at scale, sequencing, and the tooling that powers them (e.g., Apollo, Salesloft, Zapier, or equivalents).
- Analytical mindset with a track record of diagnosing operational bottlenecks and improving performance through data.
- Comfortable with ambiguity—energized by building structure where none exists, and capable of moving fast without a complete playbook.
- Strong communicator who brings clarity to complex workflows and can work effectively across Customer Success, Product, and Data teams.

### Why Join Us

- Impact: Own the team and systems behind one of Vendelux's highest-growth products—directly tied to customer ROI and retention.
- Ownership: Build the operating model, team structure, and product requirements from the ground up. This is a true GM role, not an execution-only position.
- Innovation: Work at the intersection of AI, B2B outreach, and GTM systems—shaping how companies convert event interest into pipeline.

### Benefits

- Competitive base salary and bonus
- Healthcare covering medical, dental and vision
- Work from our NYC HQ
- Unlimited PTO plus two company-wide shutdowns during the July 4th week and the Christmas – New Years week
